concept.title: Printing and PDF
concept.shortdesc: Every page prints, or saves as PDF, from a browser on A4 by default; with govuk.print=yes the build also writes the whole publication as one file for printing end to end; and with a formatter such as DesignSystemPDF it turns that file into a page-numbered, tagged PDF and links it from the site.

conbody.p: printingprint stylesheetprint documentPDFWebsites are the primary output, and GOV.UK guidance is to publish HTML first and PDF only as a last resort. The plugin follows that: the site is complete without a PDF, every page carries a print stylesheet, and a publication can be written as a single document that a browser prints whole. For the publications that do need a PDF — a standard to be cited by page, a document to be filed, a manual to be read offline — the same single document goes through a formatter, and the result reads as a book rather than a printed web page.

section.title: Three ways to paper
section.p: Each builds on the one before, and none replaces it: a publication with a PDF still prints page by page from a browser.

section.title: Printing a page
section.p: Use the browser's print or save-as-PDF command on any page. The print stylesheet hides the masthead, sidebar, search, pagination and footer, lays the content out in one column, keeps headings with the text that follows them, keeps tables, figures and code blocks whole where it can, repeats table headers across pages, and puts the page number in the bottom margin. Links to other websites print with their address after the link text, as the Design System's own print rules provide.

The paper size is set at build time with govuk.pdf.paper (A4 by default; also A5, A3, B5, B4, JIS-B5, JIS-B4, Letter, Legal and Ledger, or a width and height such as 148mm 210mm) and govuk.pdf.orientation (portrait by default, or landscape). Browsers offer their own paper choice in the print dialog as well; the build's setting is the default the page asks for. The same two parameters set the page of a PDF made by the build, so a publisher sets them once.

section.title: The print document
section.p: Set govuk.print=yes and the build writes print.html beside index.html: the whole publication in one self-contained file, linked from the home page and from every footer as "Whole publication (print version)". It holds:

ul.li: a linked contents list, to govuk.print.toc.depth levels (3 by default);

every navigable topic in the map's reading order, rendered exactly as on its own page, with headings stepped down by its depth in the map so the document's outline is a single hierarchy — chapters, parts and appendices each start a new printed page;
footnotes gathered at the end of their topic;
the glossary and the index as final parts, their entries linking to the topics.

section.p: Every id the website uses is kept, so cross-references between topics become links within the document and the index resolves without page numbers. Topics excluded from navigation (toc="no") and resource-only references are left out; a topic reached from more than one place is included once. The file is never indexed by site search, so it cannot duplicate every result.

On screen it reads as one long single-column page — useful for offline reading, review circulation or archiving. Printed, or saved as PDF from a browser, it becomes the whole publication with running page numbers; Chromium-based browsers also produce a tagged PDF with a document outline from the headings.

fontssizes in printIn print, and so in a PDF, the print document is set as a publication rather than as a web page on paper. It takes the type sizes government practice gives for documents, in place of the larger ones the Design System uses when a web page is printed:

strow.stentry: The publication's title, on the cover
Section headings: chapters, parts, and topics at the top of the map
Subheadings: topics inside a chapter, then the sections inside a topic
The lead paragraph: the cover's abstract and each topic's summary

section.p: These are defaults. A stylesheet of your own, added with args.css (), is linked after the plugin's and can change any of them: write the rule for print, on the class with .app-print in front, as in @media print { .app-print .govuk-body { font-size: 11pt } }. A single page printed from the site keeps the Design System's own print sizes.

Very large publications are not one printable document. The build writes the file only when the publication has no more than govuk.print.max-topics topic files (500 by default); above that it reports GOVK003W and writes nothing, and no page links to it. Publications of that size can produce print documents per part by building their submaps, or leave printing to the per-page stylesheet.

section.title: What the cover shows
section.p: print documentcoverbookmetaA printed publication, and a PDF above all, travels without the site around it: no footer to state the copyright, no banner to say it is a draft, no address bar to say where it came from. The cover therefore says what the site would. Under the title, the abstract and the author or organisation it carries the publication's details, then an imprint. Every line comes from the map's own metadata or from a parameter you have set; nothing comes from the date of the build, and a line whose source is absent is left out.

strow.stentry: The govuk.phase parameter, which the site shows as its phase banner.
edition in the bookmap's bookid. An edition written in words (Second edition, Version 2.1) is shown as written; a bare number is shown as Edition 2.1.
The first created date in the map's critdates; failing that, the bookmap's published date (completed, with its year, month and day).
The last revised date in the map's critdates.
isbn and booknumber in the bookmap's bookid.
As in the site's footer: govuk.footer.licence if set, otherwise the years and owner in the bookmap's bookrights. Official branding states Crown copyright and the Open Government Licence instead.
summary in the bookmap's bookrights, in every branding mode but official.
The govuk.site.url parameter: where a reader holding the PDF finds the current version.

section.p: A bookmap that gives the cover everything it can show:
section.codeblock: <bookmeta> <author>Example Standards Body</author> <critdates> <created date="2026-03-01"/> <revised modified="2026-09-30"/> </critdates> <bookid> <edition>2.1</edition> <isbn>978-0-00-000000-2</isbn> <booknumber>ESB-2026-04</booknumber> </bookid> <bookrights> <copyrfirst><year>2024</year></copyrfirst> <copyrlast><year>2026</year></copyrlast> <bookowner> <organization>Example Standards Body</organization> </bookowner> <summary>Licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence.</summary> </bookrights> </bookmeta>
section.p: Dates are shown as 1 March 2026 when written as 2026-03-01, and as written otherwise. Keep them in the map by hand: a date stamped by tooling on every build says only when the build ran. A map that is not a bookmap can carry critdates in its topicmeta; the edition, identifiers and rights need a bookmap.

section.title: A PDF from the build
section.p: PDFpage numbersDesignSystemPDFBrowsers cannot number the pages a link points at, so on the browser routes the contents list, the index and cross-references stay links, footnotes are endnotes, and every reader makes their own copy with their own browser's pagination. A CSS Paged Media formatter does what a browser cannot, and the print document already carries the rules it needs. Name one in govuk.pdf.command and the build renders the print document as PDF once the pages are written:
That is the publication as a book, made once by the publisher and the same for every reader:

ul.li: a cross-reference reads Installing the plugin (page 13), the contents list carries page numbers with leader dots, and index entries cite pages;
it can be cited by page, filed, sent and read offline, and it looks the same whoever opens it;

with DesignSystemPDF, footnotes sit at the foot of their page, each page carries the publication's and the chapter's title, the headings become bookmarks, and the file is tagged to PDF/UA-1 for assistive technology.

section.p: DesignSystemPDF is the project's own formatter, and the one to start with: it needs only the Java the toolkit already runs on, it is free and open source, and it is built and tested against the plugin's own print documents. explains how to install it and what its options do.

The PDF is written beside print.html, named after the map unless govuk.pdf.name says otherwise. The plugin appends the print document's path and the PDF's path to your command, so the command can carry options of its own.

section.title: The link to the PDF
section.p: PDFlink from the siteWhen the build has made the PDF, the home page and every footer link it beside the print version, with the format and the file's size in the link text, as GOV.UK does for documents:

A reader then chooses: the print version to read on screen or print from a browser, the PDF to keep. Nothing needs setting; the link is there whenever the PDF is, and only then. If the formatter fails or writes nothing, the build reports GOVK008W, no page links a PDF, and the site is complete without it.

section.title: Other formatters
section.p: govuk.pdf.command takes any formatter that implements CSS Paged Media, not only DesignSystemPDF: several are open source and several are commercial. Give the command as you would type it, without the two file names:

Page numbers in the contents, the index and cross-references come from rules in the plugin's print stylesheet, so every such formatter resolves them. Footnotes at the foot of the page, running heads, bookmarks and tagging are the formatter's own work: check what yours produces, and for a government publication prefer one that writes tagged PDF/UA. The plugin bundles no formatter and downloads nothing; you install the one you name.

Two limits are the vocabulary's rather than any formatter's: CSS cannot say above or below, so a page reference reads the same whichever way the target lies; and a link to a page the print document leaves out stays a link to the website.
